pages.title: v2: realism features of the new generator
pages.intro: v2 keeps v1's pipeline (ground photo, clutter, mines, camera) but replaces the parts that made synthetic images easy to spot: mines are rendered from a 3D model with their own pose, colour, shadow, dust, burial and orientation; edges are soft; debris casts consistent shadows; the whole image gets randomised camera effects. Every picture here comes from the v2 code with a fixed seed; before / after pairs use the same seed and change only the named feature, and effects are shown zoomed. Where the effect is weak or imperfect, the notes say so.

glossary.alpha: Per-pixel opacity: 0 is see-through, 1 is solid. Edge pixels get fractional alpha for soft edges.
glossary.premultiplied alpha: Colour stored already multiplied by alpha, so blurring or resizing never mixes in the undefined colour of transparent pixels (prevents halos).
glossary.supersampling: Drawing at several times the resolution and averaging down, which anti-aliases edges.
glossary.penumbra: The soft transition at the edge of a shadow; wider for low sun and long shadows.
glossary.fBm noise: Fractal Brownian motion: smooth random noise summed over several scales, used for natural-looking blotches of dust and ragged soil lines.
glossary.soil blending: Making the mine share the ground's colour and brightness: dust, a darker contact band, soil grains.
glossary.sun azimuth: Compass direction of the sun in the image: 0 deg = toward the right edge, 90 deg = toward the top. Shadows fall the opposite way.
glossary.sun elevation: Angle of the sun above the horizon: low = long shadows, high = short ones.
glossary.overcast: Cloudy, diffuse light: weak, very soft shadows.
glossary.Lambert shading: Surface brightness proportional to how directly it faces the light.
glossary.ambient occlusion: Extra darkening where a surface meets the ground and little sky is visible.
glossary.white balance: Colour cast of a camera: gains on the red and blue channels that make white look neutral.
glossary.gamma: Non-linear brightness curve; values above 1 darken midtones.
glossary.exposure: Overall brightness multiplier set by the camera.
glossary.saturation: How vivid colours are; 0 is grey.
glossary.contrast: Spread between light and dark parts around mid-grey.
glossary.chromatic aberration: Colour fringes at edges from a lens focusing colours differently.
glossary.JPEG artifacts: Blockiness and ringing from lossy compression; lower quality means stronger.
glossary.lens blur / PSF: Point-spread function: how a camera spreads a point of light; modelled as a Gaussian of sigma px.
glossary.motion blur: Smear along the direction of camera or object motion during the exposure.
glossary.domain randomisation: Deliberately varying nuisance factors (lighting, colour, noise, backgrounds) in training data so the model cannot rely on them and generalises to real images.
glossary.pitch / roll / yaw: Tilt forward-back, tilt side-to-side and rotation about the vertical axis (degrees).
glossary.face down: A mine lying on its back with its underside toward the camera.
glossary.painter's algorithm: Drawing triangles from far to near so nearer ones cover farther ones.
glossary.Sutherland-Hodgman: A method for cutting a polygon against a plane; used to slice the 3D mine at the soil plane.
glossary.berm: A small lip of disturbed soil along the line where a buried object meets the surface.
glossary.albedo: The base colour of a surface before lighting.
glossary.HSV: Hue (colour angle), saturation, value (brightness): a way to describe colour.
glossary.YOLO label: Text line 'class x_center y_center width height', all as fractions of the image size.
glossary.ablation: Switching features on or off one at a time to see what each contributes.
glossary.seed: Number that fixes the random generator so before / after pairs differ only by the feature.
glossary.RGBA cut-out: An image with a real transparency channel, used for rocks, leaves and dirt snippets.

features.title: On-the-fly mine rendering
features.summary: v1 pasted one of 50 pre-rendered mine pictures, so the detector saw the same 50 shapes and one near-constant colour over and over. v2 draws every mine from the 3D model when the image is made, with its own tilt, rotation, size, colour, lighting and dust, so no two mines are alike. A detector trained on a small pool of look-alike sprites tends to memorise them; real mines in the field never match a fixed pool.
features.how: The STL mesh is rotated (yaw 0-360, pitch/roll mostly small with a thin tail), projected top-down and rasterised triangle by triangle, far to near, at 4x resolution. Lighting is Lambert + specular from the image's sun. Scale uses the same pixels-per-unit as v1 sprites, so MINE_SCALE_MIN/MAX mean the same.

features.notes: Flat shading per triangle (the STL is faceted); no self-shadowing between body and wings; no plastic texture or moulding detail; about 35-60 ms per mine. Grid tiles are plain 200 px windows around each mine (not rescaled), so the size differences are real.

features.title: Soft edges and optics (blur)
features.summary: v1 enlarged and rotated sprites with nearest-neighbour sampling, giving jagged, hard-edged cut-outs that no real camera produces, and then added no lens blur. v2 draws at 4x size and averages down once (so edges get partial-coverage pixels), feathers rocks and grass, and finally blurs the whole picture with a lens-like kernel (sometimes plus motion blur). Without this the detector can learn 'razor-sharp pasted edge = mine'; real aerial frames are soft and slightly motion-smeared.
features.how: SOFT_EDGES: features/edges.py resize_rotate (area downscale on premultiplied RGBA, one resample, 0.8 px alpha feather on debris, 1 px erosion of Otsu masks). BLUR: features/camera.py apply_blur: Gaussian PSF sigma U(0, 1.5) px, with probability 0.15 a linear motion blur of 1-4 px at a random angle.

features.title: Cast shadows
features.summary: v1 had no shadows at all: mines floated on the ground. In v2 each image has one sun (direction, height, strength) and mines, rocks, grass and dirt all cast shadows that agree with it, and mines are shaded by the same light. Shadows are one of the most important real cues for an object lying on the ground. Rocks get shadows too, otherwise 'has a shadow = mine' would become a shortcut.
features.how: features/sun.py samples one sun per image (azimuth, elevation 15-70 deg, strength 0.25-0.65; 15% overcast images with weak, very soft shadows). Mines: the 3D triangles are projected along the sun onto the ground and blurred by a distance-dependent penumbra, plus a little contact darkening. Rocks / grass / dirt: the alpha silhouette is swept away from the sun by height / tan(elevation) and blurred the same way.

features.notes: No self-shadowing on the mine (wings do not shade the body). The background photos have their own baked-in shadows in arbitrary directions, which can contradict the synthetic sun. Mine shadows fall on a flat plane, not over rocks or grass relief. PFM-1 mines are thin, so their shadows are short (physically right). Rocks keep their rotation (rock_align_light=False) so only the shadows differ between off and on. Arrow overlay: points toward the sun; shadows fall the opposite way. Azimuth 0 = sun toward image right, 90 = toward image top.

features.title: Rock and debris seating (contact shadows)
features.summary: A pasted rock cut-out looks like a sticker unless it appears to touch the ground. v2 adds a soft contact shadow right under rocks, dirt clods and leaf clumps, a sun-direction cast shadow, and a rim blend that tints the rock edge toward the local ground and darkens the side away from the sun. Mines already had such cues; without them on the clutter, 'seated and shadowed = mine' would be a shortcut for the detector.
features.how: debris_shadow: contact shadow = dilated, blurred alpha shifted slightly away from the sun, darkening 20-50% scaled by the image's shadow strength; cast shadow = swept silhouette with capped length; rim blend = 1.5 px edge tinted toward the ground, darker on the shadow side. Rocks are otherwise rotated so their baked-in bright side faces the sun; these comparisons set rock_align_light=False so rotation is identical across variants.

The shadows are 2D approximations (swept silhouettes) and the rock photos have their own baked-in lighting, so a rock can still look flat or lit from a different side, especially with rock_align_light off. Contact shadow is weaker in overcast images. Seed 30 with leaf clumps and blades off to keep the rock clear; azimuth 120 deg in every image (arrow overlay shows sun direction).

features.title: Soil blending
features.summary: In v1 the mine sprite was pasted with a clean outline and a few hard-edged brown dots. In reality a mine lying in the field is dusty, partly coated with the local soil, darker where it touches the ground and shares the scene's exposure. v2 adds a noisy dust layer in the local ground colour, a darker contact band, soft soil grains and matches the mine's brightness to its surroundings. This removes the 'clean sticker on a photo' look.
features.how: soil.soil_blend samples the composite under the mine: (a) exposure harmonisation, (b) dust layer coloured by the blurred local ground, with opacity from fBm noise, (c) 1.5-4 px contact band inside the edge, darker and dustier, (d) thresholded-noise soil grains 0-5% of the mine, local colour. Ground dirt squares also become soft, tinted irregular grains (soil.dirt_grain).

features.title: Partial burial
features.summary: Real mines are often half-sunk in soil, so only part of the body shows. In v1 every mine was whole and sitting on top. In v2 35% of mines are buried: a soil plane (tilted up to 25 deg) hides a chosen fraction of the mine, with a rough soil line and a small soil lip along it. The label box covers only the part that is still visible. This teaches the detector to find mines from a fragment (a wing, an edge) rather than only from the complete outline.
features.how: features/mesh.py: the soil plane offset is the burial-fraction quantile of the surface heights, so the hidden fraction of the top-down area is hit exactly; the 3D triangles are clipped against the plane (Sutherland-Hodgman) and the shadow is projected onto the same plane. soil.burial_overlay adds an fBm-roughened soil line and a berm (lip) in the local ground colour. The hidden fraction is capped at 50% (BURIAL_MAX_FRACTION); the achieved fraction is stored in the sidecar.

The hidden fraction is the target; the soil-line roughness can add a few percent (achieved is capped at 50%). Boxes are drawn in green on every image below.

features.title: Colour palette
features.summary: v1 painted every mine the same dark olive-teal with tiny jitter, so colour alone told a detector 'mine'. v2 draws each mine's colour from realistic military-plastic families (olive drab, dark green, khaki, brown, tan), then adds sun-bleaching, a dirt tint and a brightness factor, so hue and brightness cover the real range and no single colour is a shortcut. Colours outside realistic plastics (blue, red...) are deliberately excluded.
features.how: features/colour.py: family by weight (olive 0.28, dark green 0.22, brown 0.20, khaki 0.15, tan 0.15), H, S, V uniform inside the family's range; with p=0.35 bleaching (S down, V up); with p=0.4 mix towards a dirt colour by up to 30%; brightness x U(0.85, 1.15). The result is the albedo that the scene lighting then shades.

features.title: Photometric jitter and background augmentation
features.summary: Real footage varies with camera exposure, white balance, sensor noise, JPEG quality and lens vignetting, and with the ground it flies over. v1 applied almost the same grain, colour fringe, vignette and contrast to every image, and gave the background only a small zoom. v2 randomises all of these per image (domain randomisation: deliberately varying nuisance factors so the detector cannot rely on them), and flips, rotates, zooms and colour-shifts the background photo.

features.title: New assets and sampling
features.summary: v1 drew from 15 background photos, a handful of rock and grass photos and flat coloured dirt squares. v2 adds many more backgrounds (indexed by family, e.g. grass vs non-grass), 34 transparent rock cut-outs, a separate layer of leaf-litter clumps (2-10 per image, desaturated and tinted towards the ground), soft dirt/dust snippets and a layer of thin grass blades, tufts and wisps that lie under and over the mines (the overgrowth partly hides mines and is counted in the labels). More varied clutter and ground means the detector cannot tie 'mine' to the few textures it saw in v1.
features.how: features/assets.py picks a source folder by weight, then a file; RGBA PNGs use their real alpha (no Otsu cut-out). features/background.py reads assets_new/backgrounds_index.json when BG_USE_INDEX is on. features/blades.py makes blades / tufts / wisps (about half generated on the fly, half from assets_new/grassBlades), sized in millimetres via the scene's px-per-mm.

features.notes: Assets are CC0 close-up textures (ambientCG, see assets_new/ATTRIBUTION.md), not true aerial photos: scale, perspective and baked-in shadows differ from the v1 photos. Leaf clumps are now desaturated and ground-tinted, which looks more natural than the earlier garish yellow/orange, but they are still visibly pasted textures; rock cut-outs have no baked shadow but receive the synthetic one. The contact sheet is owned by another agent and may be updated.

features.title: Asset audit and filter
features.summary: Before using the extra images for training, every background, rock, leaf, dirt and grass image was checked individually (186 audited). Some of the original v1 backgrounds turned out to be screenshots with stock-photo watermarks or other flaws; a detector could learn such marks as a shortcut. The audit's exclusion list is applied when the generator samples assets, and 'review' items are drawn less often.
features.how: features/assets.py and features/background.py read docs/asset_audit/exclude.json by file name: 'hard_exclude' files are never sampled; 'review' files (69) get weight x0.4 (ASSET_REVIEW_WEIGHT). v1 mode (flag off) reproduces v1 exactly, watermarks included. The sidecar records the audit status of the background.

features.notes: Findings: 186 images audited individually; 6 of the 15 v1 backgrounds and 2 of the 5 v1 grass snippets (debris1, debris2) are hard-excluded; no watermarks were found in the new assets (assets_new was cleaned: 17 backgrounds rejected, rocks / leaf clumps / dirt regenerated or defringed, six real-grass backgrounds added). The exclusion list is an auditor opinion and was meant to be spot-checked. After filtering, 9 of the 15 v1 photos remain. All images on this page use the current, filtered asset pool.

features.title: Label policy (visible-mask boxes)
features.summary: v1 drew the label box around the mine as it would look unobstructed, even when rocks, grass or soil covered part of it, so the box could include things the camera cannot see. v2 builds the box from the pixels of the mine that are actually visible after burial soil and the overgrowth layer. That matches what a human annotator would draw on a real photo.
features.how: Mine.label: with LABEL_VISIBLE_MASK the visible mask = mine alpha after burial soil, minus accumulated overgrowth alpha; box = bounding box of pixels with alpha > 0.5. A mine with fewer than LABEL_MIN_VISIBLE_PX (default 1) visible pixels gets no box.

features.notes: OPEN QUESTION: a mine fully hidden by overgrowth currently gets no box (LABEL_MIN_VISIBLE_PX = 1), so it becomes an unlabelled mine, i.e. a (rare) false negative for training; alternatives are keeping it labelled or dropping that image. A mine that is only a few pixels visible still gets a tiny box. Red = box with the mask switched off (v1 policy), green = visible-mask box. (No fully hidden mine turned up in the sampled seeds, so no example image.) In about 64 sampled 8-mine images no mine was fully hidden, so no example image is shown (the CHANGES notes report 2 of 192 mines hidden in their sample).

features.title: Face-up and face-down mines
features.summary: A mine on the ground can lie on its bottom or on its back, showing its underside. v2 flips each mine (rotated 180 degrees about its long axis) with probability FLIP_PROB = 0.30, so the detector sees both the top and the different underside shape, with the same colour, shading, shadow and burial machinery. Without it every training mine would show only its upper surface.
features.how: features/mesh.py: sample_pose returns (pitch, roll, yaw, face_down); a face-down mine starts from a rest attitude computed from the mesh's stable pose (about 1.5 deg off flat so a wing tip and the body touch the ground), and tilts of sigma 5 deg and the yaw are applied on top. MINE_POSE accepts a 4th value face_down; override {'flip': True/False} or FLIP_PROB.

features.notes: A face-down mine props one wing on the body, so its shadow is longer than a face-up mine's (physically plausible). The underside geometry is plausible but untextured (no moulding detail). The mirrored silhouette is what makes it recognisably different from face-up at the same yaw.

features.title: Whole-image comparison
features.summary: The features above combined. Same seed, v1 against v2 shows the overall change; the ablation sheet switches each flag on alone; the 3x3 grid shows how varied v2 scenes are. FLIP_PROB = 0.30 applies to the v2 mines in the whole-image pictures (so about a third are face down) except in the ablation sheet, where mines are fixed face up.

features.notes: The v1 and v2 images share a seed, not a scene: v1 mode picks its backgrounds from the v1 pool and the v2 sampler differs, so the ground and mines are not identical. Per-flag ablation images keep the same random streams, so they are directly comparable. The ablation uses 3 mines at fixed positions, burial 35% for visibility and FLIP_PROB 0 (mines face up). In the only-one sheet, the NEW_ASSETS tile (and the all-on tile) draw a different background photo because that flag changes the background pool, so compare mines rather than ground there.
